newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hungry red chips add HK banks to shopping list.
newsitem.headline: Hungry red chips add HK banks to shopping list.

text.p: China-backed red chip companies in Hong Kong have been voraciously adding assets to their diversified portfolios, and now have their sights set on the lucrative banking industry, analysts said on Thursday.

"After the handover, Chinese companies expect to play a more important role in Hong Kong's economy. They have already taken stakes in airlines, telecoms and utilities and they would like to increase their exposure in the banking sector," said one analyst at Vickers Ballas.
"Over the past years, Hong Kong banks have been very profitable and they will try to acquire stakes in local banks."

Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule at midnight of June 30 after 156 years of colonial rule. Further integration between the two economies is set to boost cross-border trade with banks braced to play a key role, analysts said.

"After the handover there will be a lot of economic activity between Hong Kong and China," said Stanley Ng, research manager at Mansion House Research. "It will obviously involve more banking activity."
This week alone, two prominent red chip companies announced plans to build up their banking activities.

China Everbright-IHD Pacific Ltd said on Wednesday it would buy a 20 percent stake in Everbright Bank of China, a financial institution established in Beijing which provides services to industrial, commercial and state-owned enterprises.
"The company's strategy is to become a broader red chip conglomerate with a focus in the financial sector," it said.
China Resources Enterprise Ltd also announced a bank deal on Wednesday, its first move into financial services, with the acquisition of 50 percent of Hongkong Chinese Bank Ltd.

Keith Wu, head of research at Peregrine Securities, noted that both red chip companies -- Hong Kong-based companies with financial backing from China -- had purchased the stakes from their parent companies and were taking on the traditional operations that their controlling shareholders were engaged in.
"They are simply trying to restructure to enhance shareholder value and to increase transparency as well as the penetration of the red chip into the sector," he said.
But their interest is expected to spread outside their parents' networks to local banks in Hong Kong as red chips become more active here after the territory's return to Chinese rule, analysts said.
"There is a lot of prestige attached to having a bank," said Alan Hutcheson, banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"I think it is partly cultural but also it is seen as rounding a conglomerate group," he said.
State-owned Bank of China does have a major position in Hong Kong's banking market, but no red chip comes anywhere close yet.
Shares of local banks have surged recently as investors anticipate movement in the industry. Hang Seng Bank Ltd led the way on Thursday, gaining HK$4.50 to HK$96.75 (US$12.50).
"Hang Seng is the biggest Hong Kong local bank. It is clearly seen as the biggest attractive target," said Hutcheson.
But he said Hang Seng Bank was too big for Hong Kong red chips, and only something the size of Bank of China or a state-owned bank in China would be big enough to buy into it.

A deal was also unlikely to take place around the time of Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule, he added. "It could be quite sensitive to start messing with the biggest bank in the territory soon after the handover."
Analysts said other targets included Liu Chong Hing Bank HK, up HK$1.10 at HK$17.10, FPB Bank, up HK$0.75 at HK$5.25, and Wing Lung Bank Ltd, up HK$0.70 at HK$45.70.
Among other banking stocks, Ka Wah Bank Ltd gained HK$2.05 to HK$11.05 and Union Bank of Hong Kong Ltd surged HK$2.30 to HK$21.90.
